deep.reconstruction:
This page has almost no text. It is a sheet of sketches drawn on recycled Cray-2 line-printer paper; the printout, dated 19 Aug 1982, is upside down relative to the drawings. It illustrates the argument of 24.12 that runs from the previous page onto the next one.

Setting. We have an arrangement (a 'system') of pseudo-lines in the projective plane, and one pseudo-line D in it. Grothendieck attaches to D:
- a disc Δ(D), essentially a small tubular neighbourhood of D thickened to the union of the closed cells meeting D, i.e. the 'zone' of D;
- a polygon Pol^(D), the boundary of that disc;
- a dual polygon Pol(D), which he decides is 'le bon', the right one.

The sketches show three kinds of local picture.

(1) Configurations around D, drawn as a green horizontal line, with orange transversal lines crossing it, sometimes several through one point (multiple points). Dashed green segments mark the boundary of the tubular neighbourhood. Near a p-fold point he labels the angular sectors 'p−1', 'p≥1', 'p≥3'. These seem to record how many arrangement edges or vertices fall on the boundary of the cells adjacent to D around a point of multiplicity p.

(2) Lens-shaped figures: two arcs meeting at two points, crossed by several transversals. The resulting cells are labelled 3 or 4, meaning triangles or quadrilaterals. Strings such as '3 4 3 4 3' and '3 4 4 3' read off the side counts of the cells of the zone along one side of D. This is the combinatorial data of Pol^(D).

(3) A vertex with a fan of grey lines and an orange arrow pointing into it, plus a red/orange line through two crossing points with a purple parallel. These appear to illustrate the 'folding' step. Boundary edges of Δ(D) next to a vertex are folded together to give a new disc Δ'(D), in which those edges become segments running from the boundary to the interior. Keeping the traces of the other pseudo-lines inside Δ'(D) creates 'artificial double points' on the boundary; the next page discusses these.

The overall aim is to rebuild the cell decomposition (the 'carte') of the projective plane by gluing the discs Δ(D) along these boundary identifications, and to compare it with the dual map. Without the folding, the gluing gives a surface with boundary whose holes correspond canonically to the vertices; this is on the next page.

The large green ellipse is probably just a schematic disc Δ(D) or a schematic tubular neighbourhood.
errors: No checkable assertions on the page; the side-count labels (3/4 cells in zones of simple crossings) are consistent with general-position local pictures.

ideas.what: Disc/polygon attached to a pseudo-line: the zone (union of cells adjacent to D) viewed as a tubular neighbourhood, with its boundary polygon and the sequence of side-counts of adjacent cells
ideas.modern_name: Zone of a (pseudo)line in an arrangement
ideas.usually_credited_to: Zone theorem: Chazelle–Guibas–Lee (1985), Edelsbrunner–O'Rourke–Seidel (1986); pseudo-line arrangements: Levi (1926), Grünbaum (1972), Goodman–Pollack

ideas.what: Folding boundary edges of the zone disc near vertices to obtain Δ'(D), and gluing the discs to rebuild the map of the projective plane or its dual
ideas.modern_name: Cell-complex surgery / reconstruction of an arrangement's map from its zones (related to wiring diagrams and dual tilings)

missed.claim: Grothendieck seems to be trying to recover the whole arrangement map by gluing the zone discs of all the pseudo-lines, using edge-folding identifications. Combined with the next page, a by-product is a surface with boundary whose holes correspond canonically to the vertices. This viewpoint is not systematically developed in the pseudo-line arrangement literature, but it is a fairly elementary combinatorial construction.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Minor. It could link to combinatorial descriptions of arrangements through local zone data, but it is unlikely to contain anything that is new in substance.

deep.surprise_reason: Sketch-only page illustrating an elementary combinatorial construction (zones of pseudo-lines and their side counts) from the surrounding text; no new result visible.
transcription_corrections: The page is drawings on reused Cray-2 printout paper; the printed text ('CRAY2 JOB 352', '19 AUG 82', banner 'CRAY2 0352') is upside down and has no bearing on the mathematics.
The '4's in the transcription look like mirrored '4's or 'ч' in the image. They are side-count labels (4 = quadrilateral cell), alternating with 3 (triangle).
The labels near the multiple point read roughly 'p≥3', 'p≥1' (or 'p+1'), 'p−1' on both sides of the green line, written partly upside down.
Upper-left label '2' may instead be a mirrored '7' or 'Z'; uncertain.
